summary: This Archives of Sexual Behavior article by Savin-Williams, Joyner and Rieger analyzes self-reported sexual orientation identity among young adults using Waves 3 and 4 of the Add Health survey (N = 12,287), about six years apart. It finds that identity stability was more common than change, that the majority identified as 100% heterosexual, and that the bisexual category was the least stable. The page is a Springer landing page with paywalled full text, so only the abstract and reference list were available.
one_line: A 2012 study of Add Health data finding that most young adults kept a stable sexual orientation identity over about six years, with bisexual identity the least stable.
key_facts: The study was published 01 February 2012 in volume 41 of Archives of Sexual Behavior, pages 103–110.
The authors are Ritch C. Savin-Williams, Kara Joyner and Gerulf Rieger.
The study used data from Wave 3 and Wave 4 of the National Longitudinal Survey of Adolescent Health (Add Health), with N = 12,287.
The two survey waves were approximately 6 years apart.
The majority of young adults identified their sexual orientation as 100% heterosexual.
The second largest identity group was "mostly heterosexual," which was larger than all other nonheterosexual identities combined.
Stability of sexual orientation identity was more common than change across the two waves.
Stability was greatest among men and among those identifying as heterosexual.
Individuals who identified as 100% homosexual reported nearly the same level of stability as 100% heterosexuals.
The bisexual category was the most unstable, with one quarter maintaining that status at Wave 4.
Among bisexual women, the most common shift was toward mostly heterosexual.
The proportion of heterosexuals decreased between the two waves, reflecting changes in identity.
Lead author Ritch C. Savin-Williams is affiliated with the Department of Human Development at Cornell University.
